arthur-glande-grand-bay.A2:
August Fichet and Ashton Page, two young white men, were brought to Mobile this morning from Grand Bay by Sheriff Powers and Deputy Sheriff Charley Cherry. They are charged with an assault.

The particulars, as gleaned from the young men and the complainant, Arthur Glande, a negro, make a peculiar story. The two met at a charcoal kiln. The whites had been invited to dinner by a friend. Later Glande was also asked to go to dinner. Page and Fichet remarked they were from Mississippi and didn't "eat with niggers." Glande took exception to the remark and an argument resulted. Page said he and Fichet were related to the Ladniers, whereupon Glande retorted, was a kin to the same wamily. Page and Fichet inferred that Glande had insinuated they had negro blood in their veins. The two whites then left and later met Glande, as he claims, and assaulted him with persimmon limbs. He claims to have been severely beaten by Page and Fichet.

The young men, after being brought here, gave bond for their appearance in the Inferior Criminal Court.

new-york-new-york-1905-08-08.A2:
VIRAGO STARTS A RACE RIOT IN HARLEM Scalps Cracked by Reserves When Policeman Elliott Was Attacked by a Mob.
Policeman John Elliott, of the East One Hundred and Twenty-sixth street station, was slashed with a razor and beaten into unconsciousness to-day while attempting to arrest a negro woman at One Hundred and Twenty-sixth street station in charge of Sergt. Lake. When they arrived they found Elliott stretched out on the pavement with three policemen standing over him, beating back with their night sticks a mob of negroes. The reserves jumped into the throng and clubbed about them savagely until their arms were tired. They also drew their revolvers and threatened to shoot the first negro who showed a weapon. When the mob had been dispersed ambulances were sent for and the surgeons patched up the wounds and cuts. Three prisoners were taken to the East One Hundred and Twenty-sixth street station and later arraigned in the Harlem Court, where they were held for participating in a riot. Elliott was taken home after his injuries were dressed.

pink-hank-la-grange-1905-08.A1:
KILLED BY QUARANTINE GUARD.
Mississippi Man Who Tried to Get Into Tennessee Fatally Shot.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]
mphile Aug 14 Pink Hane of Miss

Memphis, Aug. 14.—Pink Hane, of Mississippi, was killed last night by a quarantine guard while attempting to run the line near Lagrange, Tenn. The guard stationed on the line of the Southern Railway saw Hane, and called to him to halt. Hane ran, and after calling twice more the guard fired. The man died several hours later. Before his death Hane said that he was wanted in Joles County, Miss., but did not say why or by whom. This is the first fatality resulting from efforts to dodge the quarantine in this neighborhood.

Negro Murderer Hanged to a Tree
Negro Murderer Hanged to a Tree
A special from Glendora, Miss., says that a mob of fifty men Tuesday took Will Harris, a negro, from a Yazoo and Mississippi Valley train at Black Bayou and hanged him to a tree.
will-harris-black-bayou-1905-08-01.A3:
Got the Handcuffs Back.
Got the Handcuffs Back.

Greenwood, Miss., July 29.—When Deputy Sheriff Taylor, from whom the mob took the negro Will Harris at Black Bayou yesterday, was returning to Greenwood late in the afternoon members of the mob met him and gave him the handcuffs with which the negro had been mana- celed while in the officer's charge, and told him they were no longer needed. It was the official notification, and one as grim as it was novel that Harris had paid the penalty for shooting a white man in Mississippi.

GENERAL NEWS ITEMS.
It is now said that the object of Emperor William's interview with the czar was to obtain the latter's consent for a prince of the home of Hohenzollern to ascend the throne of Norway.

The interview with Aimar Sato, of the Japanese peace delegation, cabled to St. Petersburg, from New York, was received with satisfaction in many quarters in the Russian capital.

The official members of Secretary of War Taft's party, including Miss Alice Roosevelt, were received at the imperial palace in Tokio, on the 26th, by the emperor and crown princess, who entertained them at luncheon. The entire party was entertained at dinner at the Imperial hotel, at night, by the prime minister, Count Katsura.

John Mueller, charged with the murder of his wife and child, in Chicago, makes the novel plea of "epileptic somnambulism," declaring that he committed the crime in his sleep.

The Chicago City Railway Co. has filed a bill in the United States circuit court for an injunction to restrain the city of Chicago from interfering with any of the company's lines.

The total number of cases of yellow fever reported in New Orleans, up to and including the 26th, was 165, with 45 deaths.

Mattie and Grace Wigner, aged 14 and 16 years, respectively, were drowned while attempting to ford a creek west of Lacygne, Kas., which had been swollen by a heavy rain.

Fire destroyed the Missouri Grain Co.'s elevator, containing a large amount of grain, at Moberly, Mo.; loss, $200,000.

Baron Komura, Japan's principal peace plenipotentiary, authorizes the absolute and unqualified denial of a report that Crown Prince Yoshihito of Japan died last May and that news of his demise had been withheld for state reasons.

A mutiny occurred among the police of Panama, but it was quickly quelled and the leaders severely chastised.

Lieutenant-Commander Robert E. Peary, on board the steamer Roosevelt, bade farewell to wife and daughter at North Sydney, Cape Breton, on the 26th, and sailed away northward to reach, if possible, the North pole.

The Victoria (Australia) assembly has passed a bill granting the elective franchise to women.

William A. Cotton will decline the appointment as United States judge for the district of Oregon, to succeed the late Judge Bellinger, and will remain with the Harriman system.

Various stories are being sent out as to Japan's peace terms; but they can all be set down as mere guesses, as the Japanese plenipotentiaries are too shrewd to show their hand before the game begins.

Will Harris, a negro, charged with implication in the shooting of two white men, was taken from a Yazoo & Mississippi Valley train by a mob at Black Bayou, Miss., and hanged to a tree.

Preparations are going forward actively at Portsmouth, N. H., for the peace conference, which is expected to begin its sessions about August 5.

A tornado struck the northern rim of Racine county, Wisconsin, on the 23d inst., killing two men and damaging property and crops to the extent of $100,000.

Upwards of 10,000 persons viewed the remains of Gen. Wilman W. Blackmar, late commander-in-chief of the G. A. R., as they lay in state in Memorial hall in the Massachusetts state house, in Boston, previous to the funeral services on the 23d inst.

In the course of a conversation with Mr. Aimar Sato, of the Japanese peace delegation, in New York, the latter said the Japanese regarded America as "an ally without a treaty," and that Japan would not take the Philippines as a gift, with a bonus thrown in.

Secretary Taft and party were given a demonstrative welcome to Japan. The people of Yokohama dressed the city in holiday attire, and the landing of the party was the signal for a grand and noisy display of daylight fireworks along the streets fronting the harbor.

Judge De Haven, in the federal court at Portland, Ore., sentenced United States Senator Mitchell to six months' imprisonment in the Multnomah county jail and to pay a fine of $1,000. Appeal will be taken to the United States supreme court.

Secretary of Agriculture Wilson has recovered from his recent attack of acute indigestion.

The French minister of marine has decided to send a squadron to visit the United States at the end of October.

A search, covering several months, for a registered letter thief, who stole letters addressed to Norway and Sweden, ended with the arrest of John J. Callahan, chief clerk of the foreign branch of the New York general post office.

Gen. Thomas H. Barry, who is now with the Russian army in Manenturia, has been selected for president of the war college in Washington.

The city council of San Diego, Cal., has adopted a report in commemoration of the burial of the Bennington's dead on Point Loma, and will send a copy to the nearest relative of each of the men who lost their lives.

Jacob Solinger and J. R. Duffin, attorneys of Louisville, Ky., are charged with conspiracy to force P. J. Potter's Sons, private bankers of Bowling Green, Ky., into bankruptcy.

Attorney-General Rodgers of Arkansas has filed suit in the Pulaski county circuit court against the International Harvester Co. for penalties aggregating $600,000 for alleged infringement of the anti-trust law.

After a long and stormy meeting, the Chicago teamsters' joint council decided that the strike should go no further, and ordered all local unions that had not done so to call off the strike at once.

The most destructive wind storm ever experienced in Nevada swept over the country just west of Seattle mountain, destroying everything in its course. No loss of human life is reported, but much live stock was killed.

Secretary of the Navy Bonaparte says a searching investigation will be made into the Bennington disaster in San Diego harbor.

District Attorney Jerome of New York has begun his promised investigation of the affairs of the Equitable Life Assurance society.

German residents of New Guinea and New Britain are holding meetings and formulating protests against the establishment of a German penal settlement in the Admiralty islands, northeast of New Guinea.

In the destruction of the Arkansas Democrat's plant at Little Rock, a loss of $180,000 was sustained; with insurance of $100,000. Dan D. Taylor, a stereotyper, was burned to death.

Continued investigation of the insurance companies shows larger frauds and misappropriation of the stockholders' and policy-holders' money than at first contemplated. The accumulated billions have been used to control the government composed of the people who furnished the sinews of war for such a control, and that to a detriment of the people's interests. A glance at the columns of the daily press will produce the evidence substantiating this statement. In 1903 Mississippi paid two and a quarter million dollars into the life insurance concerns of the North and East, and in return received about three-quarters of a million for death losses and accumulations. In 1904 Mississippi paid to the old line insurance companies $2,852,495.70 in premiums, and received in return $902,946.14. This leaves nearly two millions of our money to be invested in the North and East, building up that section to the detriment of this. This two millions (and next year it will be greater), if invested in Mississippi, would work wonders in the developing of our great State. Then, why not have a Mississippi life insurance company?

Hon. A. A. Kincannon, President of the Industrial Institute and College, held a conference with Gov. Vardaman in regard to the affairs at the college. He stated that there had already been enrolled over 800 young ladies for next session, and more are clamoring for admittance. In speaking of the facilities at the college and the need for more room, President Kincannon said: "We have no funds available for enlarging our facilities but I have a plan in view whereby we can secure temporary quarters for more students if an arrangement can be made to defray the expenses. This was the object of my interview with the Governor, which was of a satisfactory nature."

Notes of Current Events.
Jersey City's census shows the population has increased 26,000 since 1900.

Sir John Tenniel, the famous cartoonist of London Punch, has just passed his eighty-fifth birthday.

Daniel Tarbox Jewett, probably the oldest lawyer in the United States, will soon enter his 100th year.

Stuyvesant Fish, president of the Illinois Central railroad, in an interview at Chicago, declared that the Illinois Central would continue to divert all grain possible to New Orleans.

Porto Ricans, representing both parties, in convention, declared for home rule and adopted a memorial to Congress on the subject.

Hyman Rosenberg of Easthampton, Mass., testifying on a charge of polygamy, said his second wife agreed to a divorce for a consideration of $28.

A mob of fifty men at Glendora, Miss., took Will Harris, a negro murderer, from a train and hanged him. Harris and his brother killed two men.

John Putanitz, a night watchman at the American Tobacco warehouse in Philadelphia, kicked a dog belonging to Harry Williams and was shot to death by Williams.

Reports from the immigration stations for the month of June show that during that month 311 Chinese applied for admission and that 300 were admitted.
